name: T4 implies Tychonoff (T3 1/2)
proofSketch: Let X be normal and T1. Given a closed set C and a point x not in C, {x} is closed because X is T1. Since {x} and C are disjoint closed sets in a normal space, Urysohn's Lemma provides a continuous function f: X -> [0, 1] with f(x) = 0 and f(C) = {1}.
source: Munkres, Topology (2nd ed.), §33 Theorem 33.1 (Urysohn Lemma); Willard §17

name: T4 implies Normal
proofSketch: By definition, a T4 space is a topological space that is both normal and T1.
source: Steen & Seebach, Counterexamples in Topology; Willard §14

name: Tychonoff implies T3
proofSketch: If f: X -> [0, 1] separates x and closed set C with f(x) = 0 and f(C) = {1}, the preimages [0, 1/3) and (2/3, 1] under f are disjoint open sets containing x and C respectively. Since X is T1, X is T3.

name: T3 implies Regular
proofSketch: By definition, T3 is a regular space that also satisfies the T1 separation axiom.
source: Steen & Seebach, Counterexamples in Topology; Munkres §31

name: T3 implies Hausdorff (T2)
proofSketch: Given distinct points x, y in X, the singleton {y} is closed because X is T1. Since X is regular, the point x and closed set {y} can be separated by disjoint open sets, satisfying T2.
keyLemma: Singletons are closed in T1 spaces

name: Hausdorff implies T1
proofSketch: For any x != y, Hausdorff gives disjoint open sets U around x and V around y. Thus U contains x but not y, and V contains y but not x, which is the definition of T1.
keyLemma: Disjoint open sets around distinct points

name: T1 implies T0
proofSketch: T1 provides open neighborhoods distinguishing x from y and y from x. Either neighborhood alone satisfies the T0 condition.

name: Normal + T1 implies T4
proofSketch: A space that satisfies the normal separation axiom and T1 is by definition T4.

name: Regular + T1 implies T3
proofSketch: A regular space that is T1 is by definition T3.

name: Compact implies Countably Compact
proofSketch: Any countable open cover is in particular an open cover. If every open cover has a finite subcover, every countable open cover also has a finite subcover.

name: Sequentially Compact implies Countably Compact
proofSketch: If X has an infinite sequence without an accumulation point, that sequence has no convergent subsequence, contradicting sequential compactness.
source: Munkres, Topology (2nd ed.), §28 Theorem 28.2; Steen & Seebach

name: Second Countable implies First Countable
proofSketch: If B is a countable base for the topology of X, then for each x in X the subfamily {B_i in B : x in B_i} is a countable local base at x.

name: Second Countable implies Lindelöf
proofSketch: Given any open cover U of X and a countable base B, for each element in U we can express it as a union of elements from B. Selecting one element of U for each used base element produces a countable subcover.

name: Countably Compact + Lindelöf implies Compact
proofSketch: Given an arbitrary open cover, Lindelöf reduces it to a countable subcover. Countable compactness then extracts a finite subcover from that countable subcover.

name: Countably Compact + First Countable implies Sequentially Compact
proofSketch: In a countably compact space, every sequence has a cluster point x. If the space is first countable, a nested countable neighborhood basis at x allows constructing a subsequence converging to x.

name: Metrizable implies T4
proofSketch: Metric spaces are Hausdorff, hence T1. Disjoint closed sets A, B have positive separation d(x, B) and d(y, A), yielding disjoint open neighborhoods U = {x: d(x, A) < d(x, B)} and V = {y: d(y, B) < d(y, A)}.

name: Metrizable implies First Countable
proofSketch: At any point x in a metric space, the open balls B(x, 1/n) for n = 1, 2, ... form a countable local neighborhood base.

name: Countably Compact is Equivalent to Limit Point Compact in T1 Spaces
proofSketch: In any space, countably compact implies limit point compact. In a T1 space, if an infinite set has a limit point, every neighborhood of that point contains infinitely many points of the set, which allows extracting accumulation points for countable covers.
keyLemma: In T1 spaces, limit points of infinite sets have infinite intersections with neighborhoods
source: Munkres, Topology (2nd ed.), §28 Theorem 28.1; Steen & Seebach

name: Compact Hausdorff implies Normal
proofSketch: In a Hausdorff space, any compact subset is closed. Two disjoint compact subsets (or a point and a compact set) can be separated into disjoint open sets by covering with Hausdorff neighborhoods and extracting a finite subcover.
keyLemma: Finite subcover of Hausdorff neighborhood pairs

name: Equivalence of Compactness Notions in Metric Spaces
proofSketch: In a metric space: (1) Compact implies sequentially compact (Lebesgue number lemma), (2) Sequentially compact implies totally bounded and complete, hence compact, (3) Countable compactness and limit point compactness coincide with sequential compactness via 1/n balls.
keyLemma: Lebesgue Number Lemma and Total Boundedness

name: T0 does not imply T1
proofSketch: The Sierpiński space {0, 1} with open sets {empty, {1}, {0, 1}} is T0 because {1} contains 1 and not 0. But it is not T1 because there is no open set containing 0 but not 1 (point 0 is not closed).
source: Steen & Seebach, Counterexamples in Topology, Item 14; Munkres §17

name: T1 does not imply T2 (Hausdorff)
proofSketch: In the cofinite topology on an infinite set X, every singleton is closed (its complement is cofinite, hence open), so X is T1. However, any two non-empty open sets have finite complements, so their intersection cannot be empty. Thus no two points have disjoint open neighborhoods.
source: Steen & Seebach, Counterexamples in Topology, Item 18; Munkres §17

name: Tychonoff (T3 1/2) does not imply T4 (Normal)
proofSketch: The Tychonoff plank [0, omega_1] x [0, omega] \ {(omega_1, omega)} is a subspace of a compact Hausdorff space, so it is completely regular (T3 1/2). However, the two disjoint closed sets A = {omega_1} x [0, omega) and B = [0, omega_1) x {omega} cannot be separated by disjoint open sets.
source: Steen & Seebach, Counterexamples in Topology, Item 86; Willard §17

name: Compact does not imply Sequentially Compact
proofSketch: By Tychonoff's theorem, [0, 1]^R is compact. However, it is not sequentially compact: the sequence (f_n) of coordinate projections has no convergent subsequence.
source: Steen & Seebach, Counterexamples in Topology, Item 105; Munkres §28

name: Countably Compact does not imply Compact
proofSketch: The first uncountable ordinal omega_1 with order topology is countably compact (every sequence in omega_1 has an upper bound alpha < omega_1, so it is contained in a compact metric subspace [0, alpha]). But the open cover {[0, alpha) : alpha < omega_1} has no countable subcover, hence no finite subcover.
source: Steen & Seebach, Counterexamples in Topology, Item 42; Munkres §28

name: Sequentially Compact does not imply Compact
proofSketch: The space omega_1 is sequentially compact, but not compact.
source: Steen & Seebach, Counterexamples in Topology, Item 42; Munkres §28
